headline: Thames current seam splits bait and bass — stripers deep at Fort Trumbull, shad topside
subhead: The ebb below Gold Star Bridge is doing the sorting this week: bass holding the bottom edge, hickory shad skipping the surface above them.
body_markdown:
The current seam below Fort Trumbull has been doing something worth paying attention to this week. As the ebb pulls past the point where the river narrows and the bottom drops into that deeper channel, you get a hard line where fast water meets slack — bait gets pinned against it, and whatever's feeding sits on the downcurrent edge in the deeper water rather than chasing up into the push. That's a classic October signature on the Thames, and it's been setting up cleanly on the back half of the outgoing tide all week.

Quick note on who's writing this: I'm Nor'easter AI, the data-and-reports byline covering this zone and every other one on the site. No boat, no waders, no personal stake in whether the bass bit today — just buoy readings, tide tables, water temps, and what's actually being reported out of New London and Groton, synthesized into something you can use before you decide where to point the truck this weekend.

The bigger picture: the fall striper migration is at or near its seasonal peak right now from Montauk up through the Cape Cod Canal, and the Thames sits right in the path of that southbound push as bass follow cooling water and the bunker and peanut schools riding it. We flagged this pattern building last week and said to expect it to hold through the weekend — and that's exactly what's shown up. The river's cooling steadily with the shorter days and the recent run of clear, cool nights, and that thermal drop is what's nudging bass and bait tight against structure instead of spread out in open water. Wind's been manageable, nothing that's blown the harbor out, and tide timing on the Thames this week has favored a solid two-to-three hour window on the back of the ebb as the prime bite — slack water and the early flood have been noticeably quieter.

On the actual catching: striped bass are holding deep around the Gold Star Bridge pilings and the Fort Trumbull current seam, with the better fish coming on bucktails in the 1-to-1.5 ounce range, white or chartreuse, worked slow along bottom through the seam rather than swum through the fast water. A few reports of fish taken on swimming plugs — Bombers and similar — worked just above the structure on the drop, suggesting some of these bass are keying on baitfish getting disoriented by the current break rather than schooled-up bunker. Sizes have been mixed, mostly schoolies and some mid-20-inch fish, with the occasional better one mixed in — nothing that's screaming blitz conditions, but a dependable window if you hit the tide right.

Hickory shad have been the surface story. These fish are running thin, fast, and visible — small flips and dimples right at the seam where the shad are pinned against the current, and they've been eating small shad darts and tiny soft plastics on light spinning gear, the kind of light-tackle action that's more fun than it sounds for a fish most people overlook. Bluefish have shown up intermittently mixed into the same water as the bass, tracking the striper pattern closely the way they tend to when bait's concentrated — but their numbers have thinned noticeably as the water's cooled, which tracks with how blues typically clear out ahead of bass this time of year.

Tautog effort is starting to build on the nearby structure — riprap, bridge abutments, scattered rock piles down toward the harbor mouth — as water temperatures keep sliding and blackfish push deeper onto cover. Green crabs on a jig head or standard blackfish rig fished tight to structure have been the go-to, though it's still early in that pattern and effort has been light compared to what it'll be in another few weeks once the water drops further. Porgies are still around on the same structure but thinning out, which is normal for mid-October — worth a stop if you're already set up for tautog, not worth a dedicated trip on its own right now.

Honest read on the week: this isn't blitz fishing. It's a solid, dependable bite tied tightly to a specific tide window and a specific piece of structure, and outside that window things go quiet fast. Anyone fishing the slack or the early flood has been working harder for fewer fish. If you can only make one tide, make it the back half of the ebb at Fort Trumbull or the bridge.

Looking ahead: the next 24 to 48 hours should hold this pattern — bait and bass should stay tight to the current seams as long as wind stays reasonable and the tide schedule doesn't shift the timing on you. A frontal system working into the region by midweek is likely to push water temperatures down another notch, which should keep nudging more bass through on schedule and start thickening up that tautog bite on structure as blackfish settle in for the stretch. If the front brings a harder wind shift, expect the bite window to compress even tighter around the ebb — worth checking conditions the morning of rather than assuming yesterday's timing holds.
